tldr: The paper introduces MABIM (Multi-Agent Benchmark for Inventory Management), a multi-echelon, multi-commodity inventory management simulator designed as a versatile MARL benchmark that can generate tasks with challenges such as scaling up, cooperation, competition, generalization, and robustness.
contributions: Development of MABIM, a multi-echelon, multi-commodity inventory management simulator with versatile, configurable task generation
Simulation of a wide range of MARL challenges including scaling up (thousands of agents), cooperation, competition, generalization, and robustness
Evaluation of classic OR algorithms (Base Stock, (s, S)) and MARL algorithms (IPPO, QTRAN) on challenging tasks, revealing their strengths and weaknesses
methods: The authors model a multi-echelon inventory system where each SKU in each warehouse is treated as an independent agent. The simulator supports multi-echelon structures with multiple warehouses and SKUs, incorporating real demand data (over 2000 real SKU demands), lead times, warehouse capacities, overflow strategies, and configurable profit-based rewards. They construct 51 built-in tasks by varying parameters (number of SKUs, warehouses, capacity) and evaluate four algorithms—Base Stock, (s, S), IPPO, and QTRAN—on scaling-up, competition, cooperation, generalization, and robustness tasks, using a single A100 GPU for training.
results: IPPO performs well with few SKUs but fails entirely at 2000 agents even after 5 million iterations. QTRAN yields good results but is resource-intensive with substantial training instability. Under competition (reduced capacity), BS static strategy suffers from overflow costs while IPPO reduces replenishment without maximizing long-term profit; (s, S) static and QTRAN show better stability. In cooperation tasks (two- and three-echelon models), pure MARL algorithms underperform, but combining IPPO/QTRAN with BS (IPPO+BS, QTRAN+BS) significantly surpasses both pure OR and pure MARL approaches, indicating insufficient upstream-downstream information exchange. For non-stationary contexts, (s, S) hindsight achieves the best normalized performance, IPPO outperforms other algorithms, and static OR algorithms perform worst, especially in generalization.
limitations: IPPO fails to converge at 2000 agents despite 5 million training iterations
QTRAN suffers from training instability and high resource demands (time and GPU memory)
Pure MARL algorithms struggle with multi-echelon cooperation, indicating insufficient information exchange between upstream and downstream agents
Static OR algorithms perform poorly in generalization and robustness tasks
The current benchmark uses flat inventory structures; tree-based or graph-based structures and partially observable settings are left for future work
